context.text: Alexandria was the intellectual capital of the Christian East, and the relation of the Son to the Father its keenest question. Around 318, Arius, an ascetic, popular presbyter of the Baucalis church, pressed the Alexandrian tradition of the Word's distinctness to a fatal conclusion.

narrative.text: God alone is unbegotten, Arius reasoned; the Son, being begotten, must have come into being: 'there was when he was not.' The Son is the first and most exalted of creatures, made that through him God might make all else, a Christ worthy of honor but not, strictly, God. Arius set his doctrine in verses ordinary people could sing, and it spread through the harbors and bakeries of Alexandria.

His bishop, Alexander, examined and condemned the teaching at a synod of Egyptian bishops around 320–321. But Arius had studied under Lucian of Antioch beside men who now held great sees, Eusebius of Nicomedia chief among them, and they took up his cause. Letters flew across the East; Constantine, newly master of the whole empire, first urged both sides to stop quarreling over 'small and very insignificant questions,' then, understanding the stakes, summoned a council of the whole Church.

significance.text: The controversy forced the Church to say with precision what it had always worshipped: that the Son is not the highest of creatures but true God from true God. Everything at stake in the Nicene Creed, and in the gospel of salvation as deification, 'God became man that man might become god', was first put in question by Arius's syllogism.

uncertainty: The exact year the dispute broke out (317–319) and the sequence of the earliest synods are reconstructed from partisan sources; the outline given here follows the standard scholarly account.
